name: The Søndermarken Oak
transport: Valby/Frederiksberg area: Frederiksberg station (metro/S-train) about 1.2 km, roughly 15 min walk; exact stop not checked.

photo.license: Used with permission from Hans Erik Lund, Dansk Dendrologisk Forening; credit required
photo.note: Viewed 2026-10-01; tree shown matches species and setting in the register entry. Credit '(c) Hans Erik Lund' by his written permission 2026-09-20.

story:
Thirty-one and a half metres is a great deal of height for a pedunculate oak, and this one in Søndermarken carries it on a single trunk 5.40 metres round at chest height. Those are the Danish Tree Register's figures, taken by the dendrologist Hans Erik Lund, who stood here on 5 September 2016, measured it, fixed its position and recorded it as alive.

Put it beside its neighbour and the numbers start to mean something. The oak we map across the road in Frederiksberg Have is 28.8 metres tall and 4.95 metres round, and it has a page of its own. This one is taller and thicker, and it has no name, no legend and no plaque. The register calls it remarkable at municipal level and leaves it there.

That is the whole of its paperwork, and it is worth being plain about what it does not say. Nobody has dated this oak. There is no planting record in the register entry and no age estimate, and a park full of oaks gives no easy clue about which generation this one belongs to. So the honest answer to how old it is: we do not know, and if you do, tell us.

The register's last visit was Lund's, in 2016. Somebody photographed something within thirty metres of the pin at the end of 2025, which in a park of many oaks proves less than it sounds. If you stand under it, tell us it is still there.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the single straight trunk, 5.40 metres round at chest height, under a crown 31.5 metres tall. It stands on an open lawn in Søndermarken, at the pin.

name: The Oak of Hegelsvej

location.address: Traffic island at Hegelsvej and Krathusvej, Charlottenlund

access: Free; stands on a small public traffic island at a street junction.
transport: Charlottenlund station (S-train, about 12 minutes from central Copenhagen) roughly 800 m, about 10 min walk; exact walk not checked.

photo.license: Used with permission from Hans Erik Lund, Dansk Dendrologisk Forening; credit required
photo.note: Viewed 2026-10-01; tree shown matches species and setting in the register entry. Credit '(c) Hans Erik Lund' by his written permission 2026-09-20.

story:
This oak has a street junction to itself. It stands on a small public traffic island where Hegelsvej meets Krathusvej in Charlottenlund, a few minutes from the S-train, with the traffic passing on both sides.

It is not a street tree in the ordinary sense. The Danish Tree Register measured the trunk at 5.23 metres round at chest height and 1.66 metres across, one single stem, and recorded the tree as living and healthy. For comparison, the oak we map in Frederiksberg Have, which has a page of its own, is 4.95 metres round. The register rates this one remarkable at municipal level, and nobody gave it a name.

It has not come through untouched. The register records that a large limb was removed on the south side, which is the kind of scar a tree collects when it stands beside a road for long enough. When that happened, and why, the entry does not say.

Two honest gaps. Nobody has recorded an age for this oak, and there is no planting date to work one out from. And the last time anyone from the register stood here was June 2013, when Hans Erik Lund confirmed the position and took the photograph. We have found no dated sighting since. A tree this size on a junction this visible is hard to miss, so if you pass it, tell us it is still standing, and if you know how old it is, tell us that too.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by where it stands: alone on the traffic island at the junction of Hegelsvej and Krathusvej, a single trunk 5.23 metres round with a large limb cut away on its south side.

name: The Oak of Hans Tavsens Park
access: Free; public park (Hans Tavsens Park), on the edge toward Assistens Kirkegård.
transport: Nørrebro; Nørrebro station (S-train/metro area) about 800 m; Nørreport about 2 km. Walk time not checked.

photo.license: Used with permission from Hans Erik Lund, Dansk Dendrologisk Forening; credit required
photo.note: Viewed 2026-10-01; tree shown matches species and setting in the register entry. Credit '(c) Hans Erik Lund' by his written permission 2026-09-20.

story:
What the Danish Tree Register admires about this oak is not its size but its shape. The entry calls the crown beautiful and symmetrical, which is an unusual thing for a register to bother writing down, and adds that the trunk carries a neat burl.

The size is respectable all the same: 4.62 metres round and 24.5 metres tall, a single pedunculate oak in Hans Tavsens Park in Nørrebro, on the side of the park that faces Assistens Kirkegård. The register recorded it as living and healthy in April 2019 and rates it remarkable at municipal level. Someone photographed a tree within thirty metres of it in November 2024.

The park holds a second tree on this map, a field maple about sixty metres away that the same register ranks among the thickest of its species in Denmark. Two different trees and two different species, so you can do both in the time it takes to cross the grass, and then carry on into Assistens next door, where Copenhagen's cemetery trees are the subject of a whole walk of their own.

What nobody has written down is how old the oak is. There is no planting date in the register and no estimate. If you know the park's history well enough to say when this tree went in, tell us.

Go in winter if you want to see the symmetry the register describes, when the crown is bare and the whole frame of it shows.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the even, symmetrical crown and the burl on its trunk, 4.62 metres round. It stands on the Assistens side of Hans Tavsens Park; the field maple we map is about 60 metres away.

name: The Plane Tree of Gråbrødre Torv
access: Free; stands in the open public square of Gråbrødre Torv.
transport: Nørreport station (metro/S-train) about 500 m, roughly 7 minutes' walk; Strøget area.

photo.license: Used with permission from Hans Erik Lund, Dansk Dendrologisk Forening; credit required
photo.note: Viewed 2026-10-01; tree shown matches species and setting in the register entry. Credit '(c) Hans Erik Lund' by his written permission 2026-09-20.

story:
This plane tree was already famous enough in 1995 to go into a book called Berømte danske træer, famous Danish trees. Its author, Qvistorff, measured the trunk at 3.90 metres round. When the Danish Tree Register taped it again in December 2013 it had reached 4.19 metres, which is what eighteen more years of steady growth on a healthy plane looks like.

It stands in the open public square of Gråbrødre Torv, Greyfriars Square, in the old Latin Quarter, about seven minutes' walk from Nørreport and close to Strøget. The tree is 21 metres tall, recorded as living and healthy, and rated remarkable at regional level rather than merely municipal. The register keeps two entries for it, an older one carrying the 1995 figures and a newer one with the 2013 measurement, and they describe the same trunk.

That makes it a tree you can watch grow on paper. Most old trees are measured once, if ever. This one has a reading from a book of famous trees and a second from a dendrologist with a tape eighteen years later, and the difference between them is thirty centimetres of trunk added in a square in the middle of the city.

Nobody has recorded when it was planted, and the square's own long history is not a date for the tree. If you know when this plane went in, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by where it stands: it is the big plane in the open square of Gråbrødre Torv, a trunk 4.19 metres round carrying a crown 21 metres tall.

name: The Oriental Beech of Fælledparken
transport: Trianglen station (metro) about 600 m, roughly 8 minutes' walk; walk time not measured.

photo.license: Used with permission from Hans Erik Lund, Dansk Dendrologisk Forening; credit required
photo.note: Viewed 2026-10-01; tree shown matches species and setting in the register entry. Credit '(c) Hans Erik Lund' by his written permission 2026-09-20.

story:
Nearly every beech you pass in a Danish wood is the common European kind. This one is not. It is an oriental beech, the beech of the Caucasus and northern Turkey, uncommon in Denmark, and it stands in Fælledparken, Copenhagen's big public park in Østerbro, just east of the Soppesøen pond.

It is a large one. The Danish Tree Register measured it at 3.21 metres round and 25 metres tall, recorded it as living and healthy in August 2013, and rates it remarkable at municipal level. The register places it fifty metres north of the corner where Frederik V's Vej meets Edel Sauntes Allé, which in a park this size is the kind of direction you are glad to have.

Telling it from a common beech takes a moment's attention. The oriental species generally has longer leaves with more pairs of veins, but from a few steps away the two look much alike, which is how an uncommon tree can stand in one of the city's busiest parks without most people noticing it.

Two things we do not know. Nobody has recorded its age or when it was planted. And the most recent dated photograph anywhere near it is from March 2021, so its life since then rests on the register's 2013 visit and the absence of any news of a loss. If you find it, a dated photograph would settle the second question, and if you know its planting history, tell us the first.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its position: 50 metres north of the corner of Frederik V's Vej and Edel Sauntes Allé, just east of the Soppesøen pond, a beech 3.21 metres round and 25 metres tall.

name: The Red Oak of Vestre Kirkegård

location.address: Vestre Kirkegård (cemetery), south end of the lawn east of the maintenance yard, Vesterbro/Valby

access: Free; Vestre Kirkegård is a public cemetery, open daily (gates and hours not checked).
transport: S-train to Enghave or Valby station about 1 km; walk time not checked.

photo.license: Used with permission from Hans Erik Lund, Dansk Dendrologisk Forening; credit required
photo.note: Viewed 2026-10-01; tree shown matches species and setting in the register entry. Credit '(c) Hans Erik Lund' by his written permission 2026-09-20.

story:
Most northern red oaks grow up. This one grew out. At 14 metres it is short for its species, and the Danish Tree Register, describing it in April 2019, gives the reason in a few words: it stands free, with a large, broad crown. With nothing crowding it, the tree spent its energy sideways, over a lawn of graves in Vestre Kirkegård.

The trunk is 3.44 metres round, which is a good girth for a red oak, a North American species that Danish parks and cemeteries planted for its speed and its autumn colour. The register recorded it as living and healthy, rated it remarkable at municipal level, and noted some water shoots, the thin sprouts an oak throws up from its trunk and limbs.

It is not a rarity and it does not pretend to be. It is a plain, generous tree in Copenhagen's largest cemetery, at the south end of the lawn east of the maintenance yard, and it earns the walk in October, when red oaks turn the colour they are named for. The Caucasian oak we map in the same cemetery makes a pair of it: two oaks from two different continents, both a long way from home.

Nobody has recorded its age. Nobody has confirmed it standing since the register's 2019 visit either, so if you go, tell us it is still there, and if you know when it was planted, tell us that too.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the low, broad crown of a free-standing oak over the graves, 14 metres tall on a trunk 3.44 metres round. It stands at the south end of the lawn east of the cemetery's maintenance yard.

best_time.label: October, when the broad crown turns red over the graves

name: The Weeping Beech of Garnisons Kirkegård

location.address: Garnisons Kirkegård (cemetery), Østerbro, 45 m in line with the south gable of the embassy

access: Free; Garnisons Kirkegård is a public cemetery, open daily (hours not checked).
transport: Nordhavn or Østerport station (S-train/metro) about 500 m, roughly 7 minutes' walk.

photo.license: Used with permission from Hans Erik Lund, Dansk Dendrologisk Forening; credit required
photo.note: Viewed 2026-10-01; tree shown matches species and setting in the register entry. Credit '(c) Hans Erik Lund' by his written permission 2026-09-20.

story:
This beech is eating a fence. Somebody once put an iron railing round a grave in Garnisons Kirkegård, the tree grew beside it, and over the years the trunk has closed round part of the ironwork and taken it in. The Danish Tree Register records it in plain words, and the photograph that goes with the entry shows the railing disappearing into the bark.

It is a weeping beech, the cultivated form whose branches fall to the ground in a curtain, and like most weeping beeches it is a grafted tree: a weeping crown set on an ordinary beech rootstock. You can see the join in the measurements. Above the graft, at about a metre, the trunk is 3.22 metres round. Below it, the rootstock is only 2.48. The crown stands 13 metres tall, and the register recorded the whole tree as living and healthy in December 2018 and rates it remarkable at municipal level. Someone photographed a tree within thirty metres of it in August 2025.

Garnisons Kirkegård is the old garrison cemetery of Østerbro, a few minutes' walk from Østerport, and the register's directions are precise: 45 metres out, in line with the south gable of the embassy beside it.

If you have already met the weeping beech we map in Assistens Kirkegård, this is its counterpart across town, slightly thinner and stranger. Nobody has recorded when this one was planted. If you know its age, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the iron grave railing grown into its trunk. It is a weeping beech, branches falling to the ground, standing 45 metres out in line with the south gable of the embassy.
